lead: Python is a programming language built on one trade: you type fewer symbols, and the computer works harder to read them. A clear two-line program does real work with no header, no semicolons and no main function. Python is free, open source, and runs on Windows, Linux and macOS. That mix made it the default first language in colleges and the default glue language in industry: web back ends, data reports, automation. This chapter covers why it exists, where it came from, and your first program.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for the idea of a step-by-step plan written before the code.

blocks.text: Every program has two readers: the machine that runs it and the human who must fix it next month. Python's design chooses the human. It drops almost everything that exists only for the compiler: header files, type declarations before each variable, a semicolon at the end of every line, a main function to hold the first statement. What is left reads close to English.

The trade is real. Python is slower than C in tight arithmetic loops, often by a large factor. Most programs do not spend their time there. They wait on a disk read, a network reply, or a person typing, and a faster language buys nothing. A shop script that reads a UPI sales export, adds the rows and prints the day's total finishes in under a second in any language; what matters is that the owner can read the script and change it.

Python is free and open source. Anyone can download it from python.org at no cost, read its source code and pass on a modified copy. There is no licence fee per machine, which matters for a lab with 60 computers and for a small startup alike.

The same program runs on Windows, Linux and macOS with few changes. Python also ships with a large standard library — modules for files, dates, arithmetic, text and network access — already installed, so a beginner can read a data file or fetch a web page without adding anything. That is why Python appears in web back ends, data analysis, automation and teaching: one language, many jobs.

Guido van Rossum, a Dutch programmer, began Python in the late 1980s at a research institute in the Netherlands. He wanted a language that read easily and still did serious system work on Unix. He named it after Monty Python's Flying Circus, the British comedy group, not after the snake. The name is short, and the official tutorials keep the joke alive with example names such as spam and eggs.

Five years carry this story: 1991, the first public release; 2000, Python 2.0; 2008, Python 3.0; 2010, Python 2.7; and 2020, the end of Python 2 support. Python 3.0 arrived in December 2008 and was deliberately not backward compatible: it repaired old design flaws, most visibly turning print from a statement into a function and separating text from binary data. Python 2.7, released in 2010, was the last of the 2.x line, and support for Python 2 ended on 1 January 2020.

One practical rule follows. Write Python 3. Any tutorial or note that shows print "Hello" without brackets is Python 2 and predates 2020; in Python 3 that line is a syntax error. The timeline below shows both lines and the long overlap, 2008 to 2020, when working code had to be checked for which version it targeted.

items: Interpreted. The interpreter runs your file statement by statement, top to bottom, with no compile-and-link step that you can see. Behind the scenes it first turns the whole file into bytecode, an internal instruction list, and then executes it; your workflow is simply edit, run, read the output.

Dynamically typed. The type belongs to the value, not to the name. A name can hold an integer on one line and a string on the next, with nothing declared in advance. Type mistakes therefore appear while the program runs, not before it starts; see 1.5.
Blocks by indentation. There are no braces. The spaces at the start of a line decide which block that line belongs to, so indentation is grammar, not decoration; see 1.7.
Automatic memory management. You create values and Python frees their memory once nothing refers to them. There is no malloc, no free and no dangling pointer to worry about.

blocks.text: Readability is the goal behind all four: short programs, obvious structure, few symbols.
Here is a complete Python program. It is the whole file; nothing is hidden or assumed.

Line 1 calls print, a built-in function that writes its arguments to the screen and then starts a new line. Its argument is the string "Hello, India", the text between the double quotes. The quotes mark where the string starts and ends; they are not printed.

Line 2 prints ten dashes. "-" is a one-character string, 10 is an integer, and * between a string and an integer repeats the string that many times, so "-" * 10 evaluates to "----------". print writes that and moves to a new line.

Save the two lines in a file named hello.py. The .py extension marks it as Python source, and hello is a name you choose. Run it and the screen shows exactly the two lines above, in that order, with nothing extra: no prompt, no quotation marks, no blank line at the top. There is no header, no semicolon, no main function and no declaration. How to run the file from a terminal or an editor is in 1.3; what the error messages mean is in 1.8.

The Python 3 bar starts in 2008 and stays open on the right, because Python 3 is still in use; the long overlap from 2008 to 2020 is when both lines were alive and code had to state which one it targeted.

spec.aria: A timeline. Python 2 runs as one continuous bar from 2000 to 2020, with 2.7 as the last 2.x release from 2010 to 2020. Python 3 runs from 2008 to today; its bar has an open right end and continues past the drawn area.

examples.question: Write a Python 3 program of exactly two statements. The first prints Hello, India. The second prints a line of exactly 10 dashes. Show the code, name the file you would save it in, and write the exact screen output.
steps: Statement 1: print("Hello, India"). The text inside the double quotes is a string of 12 characters. print sends it to the screen and starts a new line. The quotes themselves are not printed.

Statement 2: print("-" * 10). The string "-" holds 1 character. The * operator with a string on the left and an integer on the right repeats the string: "-" * 10 gives a string of 1 × 10 = 10 characters, all dashes, written "----------".
The file holds two lines of code and is saved as hello.py. The .py extension marks it as Python source.
The interpreter runs line 1, then line 2, in that order. Each print ends with a newline, so the two results land on separate lines.
Screen output, exactly: line 1 is Hello, India; line 2 is 10 dashes. No prompt, no quotes, no blank line before line 1.
examples.answer: The saved file hello.py prints Hello, India on line 1 and exactly 10 dashes on line 2.

traps: The >>> mark is the interactive prompt, not code. Typing >>> print("Hi") inside a saved file gives a SyntaxError on the first line. Copy examples without the prompt.
print "Hello" is Python 2. Python 3 needs print("Hello"); dropping the brackets gives SyntaxError: Missing parentheses in call to 'print'.
Python is named after the comedy group Monty Python, not the snake. This is a standard one-mark question with a planted wrong option.
"Python is never compiled" is false. The standard interpreter first compiles the file to bytecode, then interprets that; the exam word is interpreted, but the compile step is real.
Python 2 support ended in January 2020, so any answer using print as a statement or input through raw_input counts as outdated.

quiz.q: Who created Python, and what is the language named after?
quiz.a: Guido van Rossum created it. It is named after Monty Python's Flying Circus, the British comedy group, not the snake.

quiz.q: State the year Python 3 first appeared and the date Python 2 support ended.
quiz.a: Python 3.0 appeared in December 2008. Python 2 support ended on 1 January 2020.

quiz.q: Why does a Python program need no header, no main function and no semicolons?
quiz.a: The interpreter executes statements top to bottom, so the file itself is the program and no entry point has to be declared. Line ends mark statement ends, so semicolons are unnecessary. Headers exist to declare library functions to a compiler; Python resolves names while running.

quiz.q: Python is called dynamically typed. Explain what that means for a name such as x.
quiz.a: The type belongs to the value, not the name. x = 5 makes x refer to an integer; a later x = "five" makes it refer to a string, with no declaration. Types are checked while the program runs, so a type mistake appears at run time, not before.

quiz.q: Write a two-statement Python 3 program that prints your name on one line and five stars on the next.
quiz.a: print("Asha") followed by print("*" * 5). Line 1 prints Asha. Line 2 repeats the one-character string "*" five times, giving *****, so the screen shows Asha then *****.

quiz.q: What does print("=" * 3) output, and how many characters does it print?
quiz.a: The string "=" repeated 3 times is "===", so the screen shows === followed by a newline. That is 3 characters, not counting the invisible newline.

quiz.q: A student copies >>> print("Hi") into hello.py and runs the file. Predict the result and explain it.
quiz.a: The interpreter stops at line 1 with a SyntaxError. The >>> characters are the prompt printed by interactive mode, not Python syntax, so the parser cannot read them. The fix is to delete the prompt and keep print("Hi").

quiz.q: Student A says Python is compiled; student B says it is interpreted. Settle the disagreement using what the standard interpreter does.
quiz.a: Both are partly right. The standard interpreter converts the whole source file into bytecode first, which is a compile step, then executes that bytecode instruction by instruction, which is interpretation. The user never issues a separate compile command and gets no executable file, so the textbook label is interpreted; the compile step is internal and automatic.

beyond: Not for the exam. The default Python is CPython, written in C; PyPy is an alternative that compiles the same code further for speed, and MicroPython runs on small boards. New features enter through PEPs, Python Enhancement Proposals, permanently numbered public design documents; PEP 8 is the style guide every reviewer quotes. The official release notes on python.org list what changed in each 3.x version. Search 'PEP 8', 'Python release notes' and 'PyPy' to go further.
